source_text: In his consistit defensio nostrae opinionis secundum scripturam, secundum naturam, secundum disciplinam. Scriptura legem condit, natura contestatur, disciplina exigit. Cui ex his consuetudo opinionis prodest, vel qui diversae sententiae color est? Dei est scriptura, dei est natura, dei est disciplina. Quicquid contrarium est istis, dei non est. Si scriptura incerta est, natura manifesta est, et de eius testimonio scriptura incerta non potest esse. Si de natura dubitatur, disciplina quid magis deo ratum sit ostendit. Nihil est illi carius humilitate, nihil acceptius modestia, nihil operosius gloria et studio hominibus placendi. Illud itaque sit tibi et scriptura et natura et disciplina quod ratum deo inveneris, sicut iuberis omnia examinare et meliora quaeque sectari. Superest etiam ut ad ipsas convertamur, quo libentius ista suscipiant. Oro te, sive mater, sive soror, sive filia virgo, secundum annorum nomina dixerim, vela caput: si mater, propter filios, si soror, propter fratres, si filia, propter patres. Omnes in te aetates periclitantur. Indue armaturam pudoris, circumduc vallum verecundiae, murum sexui tuo strue, qui nec tuos emittat oculos, nec admittat alienos. Adimple habitum mulieris, ut statum virginis serves. Mentire aliquid ex his quae intus sunt, ut soli deo exhibeas veritatem. Quamquam non mentiris nuptam. Nupsisti enim Christo, illi tradidisti carnem tuam, illi sponsasti maturitatem tuam. Incede secundum sponsi tui voluntatem. Christus est qui et alienas sponsas et maritatas velari iubet, utique multo magis suas.
thought_title: Scripture, nature, and discipline all demand the veil
orientation: Tertullian is concluding his argument by grounding the veiling of virgins in Scripture, nature, and discipline, then directly exhorting virgins to veil themselves.
pass_a_gloss: In this consists the defense of our opinion according to Scripture, according to nature, according to discipline. Scripture establishes the law, nature bears witness, discipline demands it. To which of these does the custom of opinion profit, or what is the color of a different opinion? Scripture is of God, nature is of God, discipline is of God. Whatever is contrary to these is not of God. If Scripture is uncertain, nature is manifest, and from its testimony Scripture cannot be uncertain. If there is doubt about nature, discipline shows what is more ratified by God. Nothing is dearer to him than humility, nothing more acceptable than modesty, nothing more burdensome than glory and the zeal of pleasing men. Therefore let that be to you Scripture and nature and discipline which you have found ratified by God, just as you are commanded to examine all things and to follow the better things. It remains also that we turn to them themselves, so that they may receive these things more willingly. I beg you, whether mother, or sister, or virgin daughter, according to the names of years I would say, veil your head: if a mother, for the sake of your sons, if a sister, for the sake of your brothers, if a daughter, for the sake of your fathers. All ages are endangered in you. Put on the armor of modesty, draw around the rampart of shame, build a wall for your sex, which neither sends out your eyes nor admits the eyes of others. Fulfill the dress of a woman, so that you may preserve the state of a virgin. Feign something of those things which are within, so that you may show truth to God alone. Although you do not feign being married. For you have married Christ, to him you have handed over your flesh, to him you have betrothed your maturity. Walk according to the will of your bridegroom. Christ is the one who commands both foreign brides and married women to be veiled, certainly much more his own.

choices.term: secundum scripturam, secundum naturam, secundum disciplinam
choices.english: according to Scripture, according to nature, according to discipline
choices.why: The threefold authority is the rhetorical climax of the whole treatise; keeping the triple 'according to' preserves the anaphora and the weight of each source.
rejected: by Scripture, by nature, by discipline
on the basis of Scripture, nature, and discipline

choices.why: The Latin 'color' here means a pretext or specious appearance; rendering it literally as 'color' preserves the rhetorical metaphor of a different opinion having only a coloring or pretext.
'Ratum' has the legal sense of something ratified or confirmed; 'ratified by God' keeps the juridical flavor Tertullian intends for discipline.

choices.term: mentire aliquid ex his quae intus sunt
choices.english: feign something of those things which are within
choices.why: Tertullian plays on the paradox that veiling 'lies' about marital status while telling truth to God; 'feign' preserves the deliberate paradox without softening it.
'Maturitas' here means the full womanly maturity of the virgin; 'betrothed your maturity' keeps the striking image of dedicating one's adult womanhood to Christ.
'Alienas' means belonging to others, i.e., not Christ's own; 'foreign brides' preserves the contrast with 'his own' that follows.

bible_refs.note: omnia examinare et meliora quaeque sectari

pass_b_english: Here lies the defense of our position: according to Scripture, according to nature, according to discipline. Scripture establishes the law, nature bears witness, discipline demands it. Which of these does a custom of opinion benefit, or what gives color to a contrary view? Scripture is God's, nature is God's, discipline is God's. Whatever is contrary to these is not God's. If Scripture is uncertain, nature is clear, and from nature's testimony Scripture cannot be uncertain. If there is doubt about nature, discipline shows what God has ratified more fully. Nothing is dearer to Him than humility, nothing more acceptable than modesty, nothing more burdensome than glory and the desire to please men. So let whatever you find ratified by God be for you Scripture and nature and discipline, just as you are commanded to examine everything and follow what is better. It remains for me to turn to the virgins themselves, so that they may receive these things more willingly. I ask you—whether mother, sister, or virgin daughter, to use the names of your years—veil your head. If you are a mother, for your sons; if a sister, for your brothers; if a daughter, for your fathers. Every age is endangered in you. Put on the armor of modesty, raise a rampart of modesty, build a wall for your sex that neither lets out your own eyes nor admits the eyes of others. Fulfill the dress of a woman, so that you may preserve the state of a virgin. Feign something of those things which are within, so that you may show truth to God alone. Yet you are not feigning that you are married. You have married Christ; to Him you have handed over your flesh, to Him you have betrothed your maturity. Walk according to your bridegroom's will. It is Christ who commands both other men's brides and married women to be veiled—how much more His own.

problems.quote: Feign something of those things which are within, so that you may show truth to God alone.
problems.source_quote: Mentire aliquid ex his quae intus sunt, ut soli deo exhibeas veritatem.
problems.why: Latin urges not to lie; English suggests feigning (lying), reversing the meaning.
problems.fix: Do not lie about what is within, so that you may show truth to God alone.

problems.quote: just as you are commanded to examine everything and follow what is better (1 Thessalonians 5:21)
problems.source_quote: sicut iuberis omnia examinare et meliora quaeque sectari
problems.why: The English adds a biblical citation that is not present in the Latin source.
problems.fix: just as you are commanded to examine everything and follow what is better
problems.ruling: Latin 'sicut iuberis omnia examinare et meliora quaeque sectari' has no parenthetical citation; adding '(1 Thess 5:21)' misleads readers about source content.

edits.old: Feign something of those things which are within, so that you may show truth to God alone.
edits.new: Do not feign anything of those things which are within, so that you may show truth to God alone.

edits.old: just as you are commanded to examine everything and follow what is better (1 Thessalonians 5:21)
edits.new: just as you are commanded to examine everything and follow what is better

fixed: Corrected 'Feign something' to 'Do not feign anything' because the Latin 'Mentire aliquid' is an imperative urging not to lie, not a command to feign.
Removed the added biblical citation '(1 Thessalonians 5:21)' because it is not present in the Latin source.

problems.quote: Do not feign anything of those things which are within, so that you may show truth to God alone.
problems.source_quote: Mentire aliquid ex his quae intus sunt, ut soli deo exhibeas veritatem.
problems.why: Latin is imperative 'feign something', not negative 'do not feign'; she should outwardly feign married status to show inward truth to God alone.
problems.fix: Feign something of those things which are within, so that you may show truth to God alone.
problems.ruling: Latin lacks negation; says 'Mentire ...' (to lie) not 'Ne mentiaris'; translation reverses meaning

edits.old: Do not feign anything of those things which are within, so that you may show truth to God alone.
edits.new: Feign something of those things which are within, so that you may show truth to God alone.

fixed: The Latin 'Mentire aliquid ex his quae intus sunt' is an imperative to feign something, not a prohibition; the English 'Do not feign anything' reverses the meaning, so I corrected it to 'Feign something'.

problems.why: pudor/verecundia means modesty, not shame; violates glossary.
problems.ruling: verecundia means modesty/bashfulness, not shame; English 'shame' misleads reader and breaks glossary consistency with 'modestia' earlier.

fixed: Changed 'shame' to 'modesty' for 'verecundiae', which means modesty, not shame, per glossary.

problems.quote: Which of these gives custom its pretext for opinion
problems.source_quote: Cui ex his consuetudo opinionis prodest
problems.why: 'Prodest' means 'benefits/helps'; 'pretext' is wrong. Custom of opinion is helped by which of these?
problems.fix: To which of these does a custom of opinion bring any benefit, or what pretext has a contrary view?

edits.old: Which of these gives custom its pretext for opinion, or gives color to a contrary view?
edits.new: Which of these does a custom of opinion benefit, or what gives color to a contrary view?

fixed: Fixed mistranslation of Cui ex his consuetudo opinionis prodest (prodest = benefits): changed pretext clause to 'does a custom of opinion benefit'; left second clause sense intact with minimal grammar fit.

problems.quote: even foreign brides and married women
problems.why: alienas means other people's brides, not foreign ones. Also, "et...et" means both brides and married women, and "even" is added.
problems.fix: It is Christ who commands both other men's brides and married women to be veiled—how much more His own.

edits.old: It is Christ who commands even foreign brides and married women to be veiled—how much more His own.
edits.new: It is Christ who commands both other men's brides and married women to be veiled—how much more His own.

fixed: Fixed 'even foreign brides' — alienas sponsas et maritatas means both other men's brides and married women; alienas is belonging to another, not foreign, and et...et is both...and with no 'even'.

last_rejected.quote: nothing more burdensome than glory and the desire to please men
last_rejected.source_quote: nihil operosius gloria et studio hominibus placendi
last_rejected.why: 'operosius' means 'more laborious/troublesome', not 'burdensome'; the sense is that nothing involves more effort than seeking human praise.
last_rejected.fix: nothing more laborious than glory and the desire to please men
last_rejected.ruling: operosius = more laborious/troublesome; “burdensome” conveys similar sense, not a change of meaning.

last_rejected.why: 'verecundia' is a distinct virtue (bashfulness/reverence), not the glossary term 'pudor' rendered as 'modesty' in the preceding clause.
last_rejected.ruling: vallum verecundiae = wall/rampart of modesty/bashfulness; translation “rampart of modesty” matches.
